xt{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\text{\

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
{\bf Sum Invested} : Total amount required to purchase the shares is sum invested.
$$\text{Sum invested} = \text{Number of shares} \times \text{MV}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (1)** If 50 shares of FV ₹ 100 each are purchased for MV ₹ 120. Find the sum
invested.
**Solution :** Sum invested = number of shares $\times$ MV
= 50 $\times$ 120 = ₹ 6000

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (2) If you want to purchase 50 shares of MV ₹ 50 each. What is the total
amount to be paid ?

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: **Solution :** Sum invested = Number of shares $\times$ MV = $50 \times 50 = \text{₹ } 2500$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Rate of Return - RoR

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When we invest in shares, it is important to know the return on investment.
Observe the following example.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (1)** Shriyash purchased a share of FV ₹ 100 for MV of ₹ 120. Company
declared 15% dividend on the share. Find the rate of return.
**Solution :** FV = ₹ 100, MV = ₹ 120 D = Dividend = 15% per share.
Remember here, that on investment of ₹ 120 Shriyash got ₹ 15.
Let the rate of return be $x\%$
$\therefore \frac{15}{120} = \frac{x}{100} \quad \therefore x = \frac{15 \times 100}{120} = \frac{25}{2} = 12.5\%$
**If** 120 : 15
**then** 100 : $x$
Ans. The rate of return for Shriyash is 12.5%.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Ans. The rate of return for Shriyash is $12.5\%$.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (2) FV = ₹ 100, premium = ₹ 65 then MV = ?
Solution : MV = FV + Premium = 100 + 65 = ₹ 165.
Market value is ₹ 165 per share.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text: Ex. (3) Complete the following table using given information.

blocks.text:
Sr.No. FV Share is at MV
(i) ₹ 10 Premium of ₹ 7
(ii) ₹ 25 ₹ 16

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (4)** Neel has invested in shares as follows. Find his total investment.
Company A : 350 shares, FV = ₹ 10, premium = ₹ 7
Company B : 2750 shares, FV = ₹ 5, Discount = ₹ 1.
Company C : 50 shares, FV = ₹ 100, MV = ₹ 150.
**Solution :** Company A : Premium = ₹ 7 MV = FV + Premium
= 10 + 7 = ₹ 17.
$\therefore$ Investment in company A = Number of shares $\times$ MV
= 350 $\times$ 17 = ₹ 5950.
Company B : FV = ₹ 5, MV = ₹ 4.
$\therefore$ Investment in company B = Number of shares $\times$ MV
= 2750 $\times$ 4 = ₹ 11,000.
Company C : FV = ₹ 100, MV = ₹ 150.
$\therefore$ Investment in company C = Number of shares $\times$ MV
= 50 $\times$ 150 = ₹ 7500.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Ans. Neel has invested $5950 + 11000 + 7500 = \text{\rupee} 24,450.$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (5)** Smita has invested ₹ 12,000 and purchased shares of FV ₹ 10 at a
premium of ₹ 2. Find the number of shares she purchased. complete the
given activity to get the answer.
**Solution :** FV = ₹ 10, Premium = ₹ 2,.
$\therefore$ MV = FV + $\square$ = $\square$ + $\square$ = $\square$
$\therefore$ Number of shares = $\frac{\text{Total investment}}{\text{MV}}$ = $\frac{12000}{\square}$ = $\square$ shares

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Ans : Smita has purchased $\square$ shares.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (6)** If 50 shares of FV ₹10 were purchased for MV of ₹ 25. Company
declared 30% dividend on the shares then find (1) Sum investment (2)
Dividend received (3) Rate of return.

**Solution :** FV = ₹10, MV = ₹25, Number of shares = 50.

(1) $\therefore$ Sum investment = $25 \times 50$ = ₹1250.

(2) Dividend per share = $10 \times \frac{30}{100}$ = ₹3

$\therefore$ Total dividend received = $50 \times 3$ = ₹ 150.

(3) Rate of return = $\frac{\text{Dividend income}}{\text{Sum invested}} \times 100$

= $\frac{150}{1250} \times 100$ = 12%

Ans : (1) Sum invested is ₹ 1250 (2) Dividend received is ₹ 150

blocks.label: Answer
blocks.text:
Ans : (1) Sum invested is $₹ 1250$ (2) Dividend received is $₹ 150$
(3) Rate of return is $12\%$.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Brokerage and taxes on share trading

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Brokerage : We directly can't go to the stock market and buy or sell
shares, only the registered members or organization (agency) of the stock
market can buy or sell on our behalf. These members are called 'Share
Brokers'. For catering the service of buying and selling of shares they charge
some amount which is called 'Brokerage' Brokerage is paid on the Market
value of the share.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (1) Suppose if the face value of the share is ₹ 100 and market value is
₹ 150. Let the rate of brokerage be 0.5%. What amount should one pay for
purchasing 100 such shares ? What amount should one receive after selling
100 such shares ?

**Situation (I) At the time of buying shares:**
Buying price of 1 share = MV + Brokerage
= 150 + 0.5% of 150
= 150 + 0.75
= ₹ 150.75

If someone purchases 100 such shares the total cost is $100 \times 150.75$ = ₹ 15075.
Here ₹ 15000 is the share price and ₹ 75 is the brokerage paid.
**Situation (II) At the time of selling shares.**
Selling price per share = MV - Brokerage
= 150-5% of 150 = 150 - 0.75
= ₹ 149.25.

If someone sells 100 such shares, he will get,
$$100 \times 150 - \text{₹ } 75 = \text{₹ } 14925 \text{ after selling 100 such shares.}$$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's remember!

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ Brokerage is always calculated on Market value of shares.
$\bullet$ In the contract note of sale-purchase of shares, price of one share is
shown with brokerage and taxes.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:

given to the investors and compare.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:

Consult a share broker or elders in the house or use internet. Try to learn
all the terms in the statement. Discuss with your friends in the class.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
For more information :
Every broker is registered and governed by SEBI (Securities and Exchange
Board of India) Act 1992.
For keeping records of shares, bonds, mutual funds one must have
Demat account (Dematerialised Account). For sale and purchase of shares,
a trading account is a must. These accounts can be opened with banks or
share brokers. They are known as DP-Depository Participants. These DPs are
under the control of two main depositories namely NSDL and CDSL. Demat
account is same as bank saving account where shares bought are credited
and shares sold are debited just like bank pass book. The statement of
holding is given to the account holder with nominal charges when requested.
The shares held in Demat A/c are in electronic form. Saving account is to
be linked with these two accounts so that the money can be transfered as
and when required. In the same way money gets credited when shares are
sold. For opening these accounts share broker or bank representative gives
guidance.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Share brokers provide services for purchase and sale of shares for their
clients. These services are charged under GST. Rate of GST is $18\%$ on brokerage.
You can find the SAC for brokerage services.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note :- For the safety of the investors, there are other nominal charges besides
GST on brokerage. These are Security Transaction Tax (STT), SEBI charge,
stamp duty etc. Here we will only consider GST on brokerage.

$\therefore$ Brokerage on 100 share = $0.20 \times 100 = $ **₹** 20

$\therefore$ GST = $\frac{18}{100} \times 20$

= **₹** 3.60.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's learn.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Mutual Fund - MF

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have learnt that a group of persons come together to form a company. They
raise capital from the society by issuing shares. If company performs well, then
the investors of the company get benefits in terms of dividend, bonus shares and
increase in the market value gives more profit on investments. Company's market
capitalization rises. All this totality helps for the progress of the country. In short,
principle of sociology 'together we can progress' works here. But every coin has two
sides. sometimes it might happen that instead of profit an investor may incur a loss.
Can we reduce this loss ? Is there a way to reduce the risk in investments ? Yes, to
overcome this more people invest in Mutual Funds.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Mutual Fund, many investors with common objectives give their money to
the professional experts. They not only invest in one type of shares but also invest in
various other schemes. As a result, investment is diversified which reduces risk factor
and total dividend or profit is divided equally among the investors. How to invest in
Mutual Fund ? What is the rate of return ? What is the locking period ? What are the
different types of investment schemes ? All these questions could be answered by a
Financial advisor or financial planner.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
You may have heard or read this sentence that, 'Investments in Mutual Funds
are subject to Market risks. Read all scheme related documents carefully
before invesing.' Interpret the meaning correctly. Sometimes instead of profit,
investment in Mutual Fund might give loss which investors have to bear.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Mutual Fund is a professionally managed investment scheme, usually run
by an AMC i.e. Asset Management Company. They invest the money given
by the investors in different schemes e.g. equity fund (in shares), debt fund (in
debentures, bonds etc.) or balanced funds as per the investor's choice.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As we get 'shares' for the investment in sharemarket, we get 'units' when
we invest in mutual fund.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The market value of 'a unit' is called 'NAV' (Net Asset Value)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$ \text{NAV of one unit} \times \text{Number of units} = \text{Total fund value.} $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note : As the market value of share changes frequently NAV of a unit also
changes. One can redeem the units when needed.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Investments in FDs of nationalised bank or Indian Postal services are more
secured and safe, in comparison with other investments, but the rate of return
is low. It hardly helps to overcome the rate of inflation. One must remember
always that if the money is invested wisely it generates more money. For this
the knowledge of financial planning is of great help.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Investments in shares and mutual funds should be made carefully because risk
and returns always go hand in hand. So the habit of regular and deep study
is the only key.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Systematic Investment Plan

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Suppose, one does not want to invest a big amount at once, then one could
invest small amounts at regular time intervals e.g. $₹$ 500 per month could be
invested in mutual fund. Investment could be done monthly or quarterly. This
way of investment is called SIP. SIP develops discipline of savings. SIP is a
good option which in long term can achieve one's financial goals. Investment in
mutual funds through SIP for a long term is beneficial. It protects investor from
market fluctuations. One should invest in mutual fund for minimum of 3 to 5
years to get better returns and it is best if investment is for 10 to 15 years.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Benefits of Mutual Funds

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ Professional fund managers. $\quad \bullet$ Diversifications of funds.
$\bullet$ Transparency and sufficiently safe investment.
$\bullet$ Liquidity - redemption of units can be done.
$\bullet$ Limited risks. $\quad \bullet$ Advantage of long term and short term gain.
$\bullet$ Investments in funds like ELSS are admissible for deduction under section
80C of income tax.

blocks.text: Solved Examples __________________

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (1)** If the total value of the mutual fund scheme is $₹$ 200 crores and 8
crore units are issued then find the NAV of one unit.

**Solution :** NAV = $₹$ 200 crore / 8 crore units = $₹$ 25 per unit.

**Ex. (2)** If NAV of one unit is $₹$ 25, then how many units will be alloted for
the investment of $₹$ 10,000 ?

**Solution :** Number of units = sum invested / NAV = 10,000/25 = 400 units.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Random Experiment

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The experiment in which all possible results are known in advance but none of
them can be predicted with certainty and there is equal possibility for each result is
known as a ‘Random experiment’.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For example, Tossing a coin, throwing a die, picking a card from a set of cards
bearing numbers from 1 to 50, picking a card from a pack of well shuffled playing
cards, etc.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Outcome

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Result of a random experiment is known as an ‘Outcome’.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Ex. (1) In a random experiment of tossing a coin - there are only two outcomes.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
Head (H) or Tail (T)
(2) In a random experiment of throwing a die, there are 6 outcomes,
according to the number of dots on the six faces of the die.
1 or 2 or 3 or 4 or 5 or 6.
(3) In a random experiment of picking a card bearing numbers from 1 to 50,
there are 50 outcomes.
(4) A card is drawn randomly from a pack of well shuffled playing cards.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: There are 52 cards in a pack as shown below.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In a pack of playing cards there are 4 sets,
namely heart, diamond, club and spade. In each
set there are 13 cards as King, Queen, Jack, 10, 9,
8, 7, 6, 5, 4, 3, 2 and Ace.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
King, Queen and Jack are known as face
cards. In each pack of cards there are 4 cards of
king, 4 cards of Queen and 4 cards of Jack. Thus
total face cards are 12.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text:
Ace of     Ace of     Ace of     Ace of
spade     heart     club     diamond

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Equally Likely Outcomes

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
If a die is thrown, any of the numbers from 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 may appear on the
upper face. It means that each number is equally likely to occur. However, if a die is
so formed that a particular face come up most often, then that die is biased. In this case
the outcomes are not likely to occur equally.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Here, we assume that objects used for random experiments are fair or unbiased.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: A given number of outcomes are said to be equally likely if none of them occurs

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
in preference to others. For example if a coin is tossed, possibilities of getting head
or tail are equal. A die, having numbers from 1 to 6 on its different faces, is thrown.
Check the possibility of getting one of the numbers. Here all the outcomes are eqully
likely.

blocks.text:
The set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment is called the sample
space. It is denoted by ‘S’ or ‘$\Omega$’ (A greek letter 'Omega'). Each element of sample
space is called a ‘sample point’. The number of elements in the set ‘S’ is denoted by
n(S). If n(S) is finite, then the sample space is said to be a finite sample space.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Following are some examples of finite sample spaces.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Let's remember!

(i) The sample space for a coin tossed twice is the same as that of two coins tossed
simultaneously. The same is true for three coins.
(ii) The sample space for a die rolled twice is the same as two dice rolled
simultaneously.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The outcomes satisfying particular condition are called favourable outcomes.
A set of favourable outcomes of a given sample space is an ‘event’. Event is a
subset of the sample space.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Events are generally denoted by capital letteres A, B, C, D etc. For example, if
two coins are tossed and A is the event of getting at least one tail, then the favourable
outcomes are as follows.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The number of elements in the event A is denoted by n(A). Here n(A) = 3.

blocks.text:
**Ex. (1)** Two coins are tossed simultaneously. Write the sample space ($S$) and number
of sample points $n(S)$. Also write the following events in the set form and write
the number of sample points in each event.
(i) Condition for event $A$ : to get at least one tail.
(ii) Condition for event $B$ : to get only one head.
(iii) Condition for event $C$ : to get at most one tail.
(iv) Condition for event $D$ : to get no head.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: **Solution** : If two coins are tossed simultaneously,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$S = \{HH, HT, TH, TT\} \qquad n(S) = 4$$

blocks.label: Paragraph

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$A = \{HH, HT, TH\} \qquad n(A) = 3$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (ii) Condition for event B : only one head.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$B = \{ HT, TH \} \qquad n(B) = 2$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (iii) Condition for event C : at most one tail.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \mathrm{C} = \{ \mathrm{HH}, \mathrm{HT}, \mathrm{TH} \} \qquad \mathrm{n}(\mathrm{C}) = 3 $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (iv) Condition for event D : No head.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$D = \{TT\} \qquad \qquad \qquad n(D) = 1$$

blocks.text:
**Ex. (2)** A bag contains 50 cards. Each card bears only one number from 1 to 50. One
card is drawn at randomfrom the bag. Write the sample space. Also write the
events A, B and find the number of sample points in them.
(i) Condition for event A : the number on the card is divisible by 6.
(ii) Condition for event B : the number on the card is a complete square.
**Solution :** $S = \{1, 2, 3, \dots 49, 50\}, \quad n(S) = 50$
(i) Condition for event A : number is divisible by 6.
$A = \{6, 12, 18, 24, 30, 36, 42, 48\} \quad n(A) = 8$
(ii) Condition for event B : the number on the card is a complete square.
$B = \{1, 4, 9, 16, 25, 36, 49\} \quad n(B) = 7$

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Probability of an event

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us think of a simple experiment. A bag contains 4 balls of the same size.
Three of them are white and the fourth is black. You are supposed to pick one ball at
random without seeing it. Then obviously, possibility of getting a white ball is more.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In Mathematical language, when possibility of an expected event is expressed
in number, it is called ‘Probability’ . It is expressed as a fraction or percentage
using the following formula.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For a random experiment, if sample space is ‘S’and ‘A’ is an expected event
then probability of ‘A’ is P(A). It is given by following formula.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$P(A) = \frac{\text{Number of sample points in event A}}{\text{Number of sample points in sample spaces}} = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the above experiment, getting a white ball is event A. As there are three white
balls $n(A) = 3$, As the number of balls is 4, $n(S) = 4$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $\therefore$ probability of getting a white ball is, $P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)} = \frac{3}{4}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Similarly, if getting black ball is event B, then $n(B) = 1 \therefore P(B) = \frac{n(B)}{n(S)} = \frac{1}{4}$.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: $$ \times \times \times \text{Solved Examples } \times \times \times $$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (1)** Find the probability of the following, when one coin is tossed.

(i) getting head (ii) getting tail

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : Let ‘S’ be the sample space.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$S = \{H, T\} \qquad n(S) = 2$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (i) Let event A be getting head

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$A = \{H\} \qquad \therefore n(A) = 1$$
$$P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)} \quad = \quad \frac{1}{2}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (ii) Let event B be getting tail

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$B = \{T\} \qquad \therefore n(B) = 1$$
$$P(B) = \frac{n(B)}{n(S)} \quad = \quad \frac{1}{2}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (2)** If one die is rolled then find the probability of each of the following events.

(i) Number on the upper face is prime

(ii) Number on the upper face is even.

**Solution :** 'S' is the sample space.

$$S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6\} \quad \therefore n(S) = 6$$

(i) Event A : Prime number on the upper face.

$$A = \{2, 3, 5\} \quad \therefore n(A) = 3$$

$$P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)}$$

$$\therefore P(A) = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (ii) Event B : Even number on the upper face.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$B = \{2, 4, 6\} \qquad \therefore n(B) = 3$$

$$P(B) = \frac{n(B)}{n(S)}$$

$$\therefore P(B) = \frac{3}{6} = \frac{1}{2}$$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (3)** A card is drawn from a well shuffled pack of 52 playing cards. Find the
probability of each event. The card drawn is (i) a red card (ii) a face card
**Solution :** ‘S’ is the sample space. $\therefore$ n(S) = 52

Event A : Card drawn is a red card.

Total red cards = 13 hearts + 13 diamonds = 26

$\therefore$ n(A) = 26

$\therefore$ P(A) = $\frac{\text{n(A)}}{\text{n(S)}} = \frac{26}{52} = \frac{1}{2}$

Event B : Card drawn is a face card.

Total face cards = 12 $\therefore$ n(B) = 12

$\therefore$ P(B) = $\frac{\text{n(B)}}{\text{n(S)}} = \frac{12}{52} = \frac{3}{13}$

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
**Ex. (4)** A box contains 5 strawberry chocolates, 6 coffee chocolates and 2 peppermint
chocolates. Find the probability of each of the following events, if one of the
chocolates is picked from the box at random. (i) it is a coffee chocolate.
(ii) it is a peppermint chocolate.

**Solution :** Sample space is ‘S’ and $n(S) = 5 + 6 + 2 = 13$

Event A : it is a coffee chocolate | Event B : it is a peppermint chocolate

$\therefore \quad n(A) = 6$ | $\therefore \quad n(B) = 2$

$\therefore \quad P(A) = \frac{n(A)}{n(S)} = \frac{6}{13}$ | $\therefore \quad P(B) = \frac{n(B)}{n(S)} = \frac{2}{13}$

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
**Let's remember!**

$\bullet$ The Probability is expressed as a fraction or a percentage.
$\bullet$ The probability of any event is from 0 to 1 or 0% to 100%.
If E is any event, $0 \le P(E) \le 1$ or 0 % $\le P(E) \le 100$ %.
e.g. probability $\frac{1}{4}$ is written as 25 %.
$\bullet$ This lesson began with a discussion of 40 chits with names of plants and each of
40 students picking a chit. Only one chit had the name Basil on it. The probability
of any student getting the chit of Basil is $\frac{1}{40}$ . For a student standing first or last
in the row, or anywhere in between, the probability is the same.

blocks.label: Chapter-title
blocks.text: 6 Statistics

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's study.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ Measures of a central tendency-
mean, median and mode from grouped frequency table.
$\bullet$ Graphical representation of statistical data -
histogram, frequency polygon, pie diagram

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Statistics is useful in many fields of life: for example, agriculture, economics,
commerce, medicine, botany, biotechnology, physics, chemistry, education, sociology,
administration etc. An experiment can have many outcomes. To assess the possibility
of possible outcomes, one has to carry out the experiment on a large scale and keep
the record meticulously. Possibilities of different outcomes can be assessed using
the record. For this purpose, rules are formulated in statistics.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Francis Galton (1822-1911) has done much of fundamental work in
statistics.He used to prepare questionnaires, distribute
them among people and request them to fill them up.
He collected information from a number of people
and recorded their backgrounds, financial situations,
likes and dislikes, health etc. on a large scale. By that
time, it was known that the fingerprints of different
people are different. He collected finger-prints of a
large number of people and invented a method of their
classification. Using statistical methods, he showed that the possibility of
finger prints of two different people being identical is nearly zero. This result
made it possible to identify a person from his finger-prints. This method of
identifying criminals was accepted in the judiciary. He had done much work
in the field of anthropology of humans and other animals also.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's recall.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We usually find a specific property in the numerical data collected in a survey
that the scores have a tendency to cluster around a particular score. This score is
a representative number of the group. The number is called the measure of central
tendency.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the previous standards we have studied the measures of central tendency,
namely the mean, median and mode, for ungrouped data.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 1 : Measure the height in cm of all students in your class. We find that
the heights of many students cluster near a specific number.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Activity 2 : Collect a number of fallen leaves of a peepal tree. Distribute the
leaves among the students and ask them to measure the lengths of them. Record
the lengths. We notice that their lengths tend to cluster around a number.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now we are going to do some more study of the mean, median and mode. Let
us know the symbols and the terminology required for it.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
The mean of statistical data = $\frac{\text{The sum of all scores}}{\text{Total no. of scores}} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i}{N}$
(Here $x_i$ is the $i^{\text{th}}$ score)

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Mean is denoted by $\overline{\text{X}}$ and it represents the average of the given data.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \overline{X} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i}{N} $$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's learn.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Mean from classified frequency distribution

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When the number of scores in a data is large, it becomes tedious to write all
numbers in the above formula and take their sum. So we use some different methods
to find the sum.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Sometimes, the large data collected from an experiment is presented in a table
in the grouped form. In such a case, we cannot find the exact mean of statistical data.
Hence, let us study a method which gives the approximate mean, or a number nearby.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Assumed mean method

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
In the examples solved above, we see that some times the product $x_i f_i$ is
large. Hence it becomes difficult to calculate the mean by direct method. So let us
study another method, called the 'assumed mean method'. Finding the mean becomes
simpler if we use addition and division in this method.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: For example, we have to find the mean of the scores 40, 42, 43, 45, 47 and 48.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The obeservation of the scores reveals that the mean of the data is more than
40. So let us assume that the mean is 40. $40-40 = 0$, $42 - 40 = 2$, $43-40 = 3$,
$45-40 = 5$, $47 - 40 = 7$, $48 - 40 = 8$ These are called 'deviations'. Let us find
their mean. Adding this mean to the assumed mean, we get the mean of the data.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: That is, mean $=$ assumed mean $+$ mean of the deviations

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Using the symbols-

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A- for assumed mean; $d$- for deviation and $\overline{d}$ - for the mean of the deviations,
the formula for mean of the given data can be briefly written as $\overline{\text{X}} = \text{A} + \overline{d}$ .

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us solve the same example taking 43 as assumed mean. For this, let us find
the deviations by subtracting 43 from each score.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The sum of the deviations $= -3 -1 + 0 + 2 + 4 + 5 = 7$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Now, $\overline{\mathrm{X}}=\mathrm{A}+\overline{d}$
$=43+\left(\frac{7}{6}\right)$ (as the number of deviations is 6)
$=43+1 \frac{1}{6}=44 \frac{1}{6}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Note that; use of assumed mean method reduces the work of calculations.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Also note that; taking any score, or any other convenient number as asssumed
mean does not change the mean of the data.

blocks.label: Section-title

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We studied the direct method and assumed mean method to find the mean. Now
we study one more method which reduces the calculations still further.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ Find the values of $d_i$ as $d_i = x_i$ - A and write in the column.


$\bullet$ If we can find $g$, the G.C.D. of all $d_i$ easily, we create a column for all $u_i$ where

blocks.text: Let's recall.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
There was a science exhibition in a city for two days. A school sent two boys
and two girls to participate in the exhibition. There were ten hotels, within a distance
of one kilometer, from the venue of exhibition. Their rates of meals, in the ascending
order were rupees 40, 45, 60, 65, 70, 80, 90, 100 and 500. They had to choose one of
them for the dinner.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The average of rates in all the hotels was $\text{\rupee}$ $\frac{1130}{10} = 113$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Which hotel do you think they chose? Except the rate ₹ 500, all others were
less than ₹ 113. The students decided to choose a hotel having medium rate. The first
day they chose the hotel with rate ₹ 70 and on the next day, the hotel with the rate
₹ 80/-.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: This example shows that sometimes the median is used instead of the mean.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the previous standard we have studied the concept of a median.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ If the numbers in a data are arranged in the ascending order, the number at the
middle position is called the median of the data.

$\bullet$ The median divides the array of numbers in two equal parts, that is the number of
scores below and above the median is equal.

$\bullet$ The scores are written as $k_1 \le k_2 \le k_3 \dots \le k_n$.

$\bullet$ If the number of scores is odd, then the $\frac{n+1}{2}$ th score is the median of the data. That
is, the number of scores below as well as above $k_{\frac{n+1}{2}}$ is $\frac{n-1}{2}$ ; verify the fact by
taking $n = 2m + 1$.

$\bullet$ If the number of the scores is even, then the mean of the middle two terms is the
median. This is because the number of terms below $k_{\frac{n}{2}}$ and above $k_{\frac{n+2}{2}}$ is equal,
which is $\frac{n-2}{2}$. Verify this by taking $n = 2m$.

$\bullet$ Hence the mean of $\frac{n}{2}$ th and $\frac{n+2}{2}$ th term is the median of the data.

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (1) In 32, 33, 38, 40, 43, 48, 50; the fourth number is at the middle. Hence the
median of the data is 40
Ex. (2) In 61, 62, 65, 66, 68, 70, 74, 75 ; the number of scores is 8, that is even.
Therefore, the fourth and the fifth numbers are at the middle, which are 66 and
68. Hence the median = $\frac{66+68}{2} = 67$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's learn.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Median for grouped frequency distribution

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
When the number of scores in a data is large, it is difficult to arrange them in
ascending order. In such case, the data is divided into groups. So let us study, with an
example, how the median of grouped data is found.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Ex. The scores 6, 8, 10.4, 11, 15.5, 12, 18 are grouped in the following table.

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Class Tally Marks Frequency Class Tally Marks Frequency
6-10 || 2 5.5-10.5 ||| 3
11-15 || 2 10.5-15.5 || 2
16-20 | 1 15.5-20.5 || 2

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We could not record the scores 10.4 and 15.5 in the first table, as they
cannot be placed in any of the classes 6-10, 11-15, 16-20. We know that in
such a case the classes are made continuous.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For this, in the first table, the lower class limits are reduced by $0.5$ and
the upper class limits are increased by $0.5$ and the second table is prepared. In
the second table, the score $15.5$ is placed in the class $15.5-20.5$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Note that if the method of making groups is changed, the frequency
distribution may change.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Let's remember!

In the above table, the class mark of $6-10$ is $= \frac{6+10}{2} = \frac{16}{2} = 8$;
Similarly, the class mark of $5.5-10.5$ is $= \frac{5.5+10.5}{2} = \frac{16}{2} = 8$.
This shows that, if the classes are made continuous, the class marks do not
change

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Solved Example :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The following table shows frequency distribution of marks of 100 students of $10^{\text{th}}$
class which they obtained in a practice examination. Find the median of the marks.

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Marks in exam 0-20 20-40 40-60 60-80 80-100
No. of students 4 20 30 40 6

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Solution : $N = 100$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\therefore \frac{N}{2} = 50$. Hence the $50^{\text{th}}$ number will be the approximate median. Hence we
have to find out the class which contains the $50^{\text{th}}$ term. Writing the cumulative
frequencies less than the upper limit, we can find it.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: So, let us prepare less than cumulative frequency distribution table.

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Class
(Student's marks )		 No. of students
fi		 Cumulaive frequency
less than the
upper limit
cf
0-20 4 4
20-40 20 24
40-60 30 54
60-80 40 94
80-100 6 100

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
$\bullet$ From the table, the $50^{\text{th}}$ score is in the class $40-60$. The class which contains
the median, is called the **median class**. So, here $40-60$ is the median class.

$\bullet$ The lower class limit of $40-60$ is $40$. Its frequency is $30$.

$\bullet$ Out of the first $50$ scores, $24$ scores are less than $40$. The remaining
$50 - 24 = 26$ are in class $(40-60)$. The $50^{\text{th}}$ score in that class is estimated as
follows.

$\bullet$ $26$ out of $30$ scores in the class $40-60$, are upto the $50^{\text{th}}$ score and the class
interval is $20$. So it is assumed that, the $50^{\text{th}}$ score is more than $40$ by $\frac{26}{30} \times 20$.

$\therefore$ it is approximately $40 + \frac{26}{30} \times 20 = 40 + \frac{52}{3} = 57\frac{1}{3}$.

$\therefore$ median $= 57\frac{1}{3}$

blocks.label: List
blocks.text: • We can formulate this as follows,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{Median} = L + \left[ \frac{\frac{N}{2} - cf}{f} \right] \times h $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the formula,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$L = \text{Lower class limit of the median class,}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$N = \text{Sum of frequencies}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$h = \text{Class interval of the median class,}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$f = \text{Frequency of the median class}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $$cf = \text{Cumulative frequency of the class preceding the median class.}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the above example; $\frac{N}{2} = 50$, $cf = 24$, $h = 20$, $f = 30$, $L = 40$,

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ \text{Median} = L + \left[ \frac{\frac{N}{2} - cf}{f} \right] \times h \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \ . \text{ (Formula)} $$

$$ = 40 + \left( \frac{50 - 24}{30} \right) \times 20 $$

$$ = 40 + \frac{26 \times 20}{30} $$

$$ = 40 + 17 \frac{1}{3} $$

$$ = 57 \frac{1}{3} $$

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Let's remember!

$\blacklozenge$ If the given classes are not continuous, we have to make them
continuous to find out the median.
$\blacklozenge$ It is difficult to write the scores in the ascending order when the
number of scores is large. So the data is classified into groups. It
is not possible to find the exact median of a classified data, but
the approximate median is found by the formula.

$$Median = L + \left[ \frac{\frac{N}{2} - cf}{f} \right] \times h$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$\therefore$ Let us subtract $1 \div 2 = 0.5$ from the lower class limit of each class
and add to the upper class limit of each class, and make the classes continuous.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
(2) Make a column of cumulative frequency 'less than' in the new table
showing the continuous classes.

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Given
Class		 Continuous
classes		 Frequency
$f_i$		 Cumulative frequency
less than
200-209 199.5-209.5 4 4
210-219 209.5-219.5 14 18 $\rightarrow$ cf
220-229 219.5-229.5 26 $\rightarrow$ $f$ 44
230-239 229.5-239.5 10 54
240-249 239.5-249.5 6 60

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Here, total of frequencies $= \Sigma f_i = \mathrm{N} = 60 \therefore \frac{N}{2} = 30.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ 30th score is the approximate median.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
First 18 scores are less than 219.5 and the remaining, $30 - 18 = 12$ scores
are in the class $219.5 - 229.5$. Therefore, $219.5 - 229.5$ is the median class.
The cumulative frequency of the class 219.5-229.5 is 44.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the formula,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$$L = \text{Lower class limit} = 219.5, h = \text{Class interval of the median class} = 10$$
$$cf = \text{The frequency of the class preceding the median class} = 18,$$
$$f = \text{The frequency of the median class} = 26$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \text{Median} = L + \left[ \frac{\frac{N}{2} - cf}{f} \right] \times h $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ The median of the distance travelled is $= 224.12$ Km

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (2) The following table shows the ages of persons who visited a museum
on a certain day. Find the median age of the persons visiting the museum.

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Age (Years) No. of persons
Less than 10 3
Less than 20 10
Less than 30 22
Less than 40 40
Less than 50 54
Less than 60 71

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Solution :** The given cumulative frequency table is of the 'less than' form. So,
we will have to decide the true class limits first. We know that, the 'less
than' cumulative frequency is associated with the upper class limits. The
upper class limit of the first class is 10. The age of any person is a
positive number, so the first class must be 0-10. The upper class limit
of the next class is 20, so the second class must be 10-20. In this way,
make the classes of interval 10. In this way the last class is 50-60. So
the given table can now be rewritten as follows.

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Age (years) Class No. of persons
(Frequency)		 Cumulative frequency
Less than
Less than 10 0-10 3 3
Less than 20 10-20 10 - 3 = 7 10
Less than 30 20-30 22 - 10 = 12 22 \rightarrow cf
Less than 40 30-40 40 - 22 = 18 \rightarrow f 40
Less than 50 40-50 54 - 40 = 14 54
Less than 60 50-60 71 - 54 = 17 71

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Here $N = 71 \therefore \frac{N}{2} = 35.5$ and $h = 10$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The number 35.5 is in the class 30-40, hence it is the median class. The
cumulative frequency of its preceding class is 22, $\therefore cf = 22, L = 30, f = 18.$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ the median age of the persons visiting the museum is $= 37.5$ years

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's learn.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Mode for grouped frequency distribution

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We know that the score repeating maximum number of times in a data
is called the mode of the data.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
For example, a company manufactures bicycles of different colours. To know which
colour is most wanted, the company needs to know the mode. If a company
manufactures many items, it may want to know which item sells most. In such
cases, the mode is needed.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We have learnt the method of finding the mode of an ungrouped data.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Now let us study the method of estimation of mode of grouped data.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: The following formula is used for the purpose.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: Mode = $L + \left[ \frac{f_1 - f_0}{2f_1 - f_0 - f_2} \right] \times h$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: In the above formula,

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
$$L = \text{Lower class limit of the modal class.}$$

$$f_1 = \text{Frequency of the modal class.}$$

$$f_0 = \text{Frequency of the class preceding the modal class.}$$

$$f_2 = \text{Frequency of the class succeeding the modal class.}$$

$$h = \text{Class interval of the modal class.}$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Let us see, with an example, how the mode is estimated using the above
formula.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: $$ \text{\textit{Solved}} \quad \text{Examples} \quad \text{\textit{Solved}} $$

Ex. (2) The following frequency distribution table shows the classification of

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Petrol filled (Litre) 1-3 4-6 7-9 10-12 13-15
No. of vehicle 33 40 27 18 12

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Solution : The given classes are not continuous. So, let us make them contin-
uous and rewrite the table.

blocks.label: Table
blocks.text:
Class Continuous classes Frequency
1-3 0.5-3.5 33 \rightarrow f_0
4-6 3.5-6.5 40 \rightarrow f_1
7-9 6.5-9.5 27 \rightarrow f_2
10-12 9.5-12.5 18
13-15 12.5-15.5 12

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:

Mode = $3.5 + \left[ \frac{40 - 33}{2(40) - 33 - 27} \right] \times h$

$\quad \quad \quad = 3.5 + \left[ \frac{7}{80 - 60} \right] \times 3$

$\quad \quad \quad = 3.5 + \frac{21}{20}$

$\quad \quad \quad = 3.5 + 1.05$

$\quad \quad \quad = 4.55$

blocks.label: Paragraph

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Let's remember!

We have studied the central tendencies mean, median and mode. Before
selecting any of these measures, we have to know the purpose of its selection
clearly.
   Suppose, we have to judge the performance of five divisions of standard
10 in the internal examination. For the purpose, we have to find the 'mean'
of marks of students in each division.
   If we have to make two groups of students in a division based on their
marks in the examination, we have to find the 'median' of their marks
   If a 'bachat' group producing chalks wants to know about the colour of
chalks having maximum demand, it will have to choose the 'mode'.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Pictorial representation of statistical data

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
The mean, median or mode of a numerical data or analysis of the
data is useful to draw some useful inferences.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We know that tabulation is one of the methods of representing numerical
data in brief. But a table does not quickly reveal some aspects of the data. A
common man is interested in the important aspects of a data. For example,
annual budget, information about a game, etc. Let us think of another way of
data representation for the purpose.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: Presentation of data

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Pictorial and graphical presentation are attractive methods of data interpretation.
The tree chart below shows different methods of data interpretation.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
We have studied some of these methods and graphs in previous standards. Now we
will learn a histogram, a frequency polygon and a pie diagram.

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Florence Nightingale (1820-1910) The lady is
considered as an idol in the field of nursing. She was
devoted to the work of caring for the wounded and
the sick. In the crimean war, she nursed wounded
soldiers and saved their lives. She is also known
for her fundamental work is the field of statistics.
She kept a systematic record of the conditions of
wounded soldiers, treatments given to them and
the results of the treatments and deduced important
conclusions. The cause of the death of soldiers was more often a disease
like typhoid or cholera and not the wounds in the war. The causes of the
diseases were lack of cleanliness of the surrounding, polluted water and
crowded dwelling of the patients. Florence exhibited the information in
the form of graphs, and pie charts to convince the people. She showed
that proper treatments and observing the rules of cleanliness decreases the
death rate considerably. The municipalities accepted her observations, that
to maintain the hygiene of town, good drainage system and clean drinking
water for everyone are necessary. Her work established that systematic
records and the statistical methods are useful in drawing reliable inferences.

blocks.label: Paragraph

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Many times we find information of different types in newspapers given in
the form of pie diagrams. For example, the annual budget, performance of different
nations in olympic games, etc.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
Now we shall see, by examples, how to interpret the information from a pie
diagram.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Example :

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
As deduced from a survey, the classification of skilled workers is shown in the pie
diagram (fig 6.11). If the number of workers in the production sector is 4500, answer
the following questions.

blocks.label: Image-caption
blocks.text: fig 6.11

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
(i) What is the total number of skilled
workers in all fields ?

(ii) What is the number of skilled workers
in the field of constructions ?

(iii) How many skilled workers are in
agriculture ?

(iv) Find the difference between the
numbers of workers in the field of
production and construction.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
**Solution :** (i) Suppose, the total number of skilled workers in all fields is $x$.
$\therefore$ the central angle for $x$ persons is $= 360^{\circ}$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Central angle for number of persons in production field

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$$ = \frac{\text{Number of persons in production field}}{x} \times 360 $$

$$ \therefore 90 = \frac{4500}{x} \times 360 $$

$$ \therefore x = 18000 $$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ total number of skilled workers in all the fields together $= 18000$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (ii) The angle shown for construction sector $= 72^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \therefore 72 = \frac{\text{Number of persons in construction}}{18000} \times 360 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\therefore$ number of persons in construction field $= \frac{72 \times 18000}{360}$
$= 3600$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: (iii) The central angle for agriculture field is $24^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \therefore 24 = \frac{\text{Number of workers in agriculture}}{\text{total skilled workers}} \times 360 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$24 = \frac{\text{Number of workers in agriculture}}{18000} \times 360$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
$\therefore$ number of workers in agriculture $= \frac{24 \times 18000}{360}$
$= 1200$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
(iv) The difference between angles relating fields of production and construction
$= 90^{\circ} - 72^{\circ} = 18^{\circ}$.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: $\therefore$ The difference between the central angles =

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$ \frac{\text{Difference between numbres of workers in the fields}}{\text{Total number of skilled workers}} \times 360 $$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text: $$18 = \frac{\text{Difference between the numbers of workers in the fields}}{18000} \times 360$$

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
Difference between the numbers of workers in the two fields $= \frac{18 \times 18000}{360}$
$= 900$

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's remember!

blocks.label: Infobox
blocks.text:
Let's remember!

$\bullet$ Every component of a data is shown by a sector associated with it.
$\bullet$ The measure of the central angle of the sector is in proportion with the
number of scores in that component.
$\bullet$ The measure of central angle $(\theta) = \frac{\text{Number of scores in component}}{\text{Total number of scores}} \times 360^0$
$\bullet$ A circle of suitable radius should be drawn. Divide the circle in sectors
such that the measure of central angle of each sector is proportional to
the number of scores in its corresponding component in the data.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Let's learn.

blocks.label: Section-title
blocks.text: To draw a Pie diagram

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: We have seen how to read a pie diagram. Now let us learn to draw it.

blocks.label: List
blocks.text:
1. To draw a pie diagram, the whole circle is divided into sectors proportional to the
components of the data
2. The measure of central angle of each sector is found by the following formula.

blocks.label: Equation
blocks.text:
The measure of central angle of sector $\theta$
$$= \frac{\text{Number of scores in the components}}{\text{Total number of scores}} \times 360$$

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text:
A circle of a suitable radius is drawn. Then it is divided into sectors such that,
the number of sectors is equal to the number of components in the data.

blocks.label: Paragraph
blocks.text: Let us understand the method through examples.

blocks.label: Sub-section-title
blocks.text: Solved Examples 333

blocks.label: Solved-example
blocks.text:
Ex. (1) In a bicycle shop, number of bicycles purchased and choice of their colours was as follows. Find the measures of sectors of a circle to show the information by a pie diagram. Solution : In all 36 bicycles were purchased. Out of them 10 bicycles were white coloured. $\therefore$ the measure of sector showing white coloured bicycles $$ = \frac{\text{Number of white bicycles}}{\text{Total number of bicycles}} \times 360 $$ $$ = \frac{10}{36} \times 360 = 100 $$ The measures of angles of sector relating to bicycles of other colours can be calculated similarly which are shown in the adjacent table.
Colour Number of
bicycles		 Central angle of
the sector
White 10 $\frac{10}{36} \times 360^{\circ} = 100^{\circ}$
Black 9 $\frac{9}{36} \times 360^{\circ} = 90^{\circ}$
Blue 6 $60^{\circ}$
Grey 7 $70^{\circ}$
Red 4 $40^{\circ}$
Total 36 $360^{\circ}$

Shops 5 $\frac{5}{60} \times 360 = 30^{\circ}$
Offices 6 $\frac{6}{60} \times 360 = 36^{\circ}$

one by one, in the clockwise direction. (While drawing the sectors one by one,
